profile.name: Maypole Dance (Jamaica)
profile.tagline: Traditional Jamaican Maypole dance featuring mento music
profile.insight: The Jamaican Maypole Dance emerged during slavery and post-emancipation, incorporating mento music and sharing visual and stylistic elements with mento dance.
profile.profile: The Maypole Dance in Jamaica is one of the island's traditional dance forms that emerged during the eras of slavery and post-emancipation. It is traditionally accompanied by mento music, an acoustic folk style born from African and European fusions. Elements of mento dance can be observed in Maypole performances alongside other traditional forms like quadrille and jonkunnu. Beyond its historical emergence, detailed technical descriptions of the dance choreography are not present in the sources.
profile.profile_long: The Maypole Dance in Jamaica is documented as one of the island's traditional dance forms that emerged during slavery and post-emancipation. These cultural traditions and dance forms feature mento music, which is Jamaica's first commercially recorded music style originating in the 19th century through a fusion of African rhythmic elements and European folk traditions. Elements of mento dance—characterized by lively, informal movements, bent knees, and footwork—may be seen in Jamaican quadrille, Maypole, and jonkunnu performances. Detailed technical descriptions of the Maypole Dance's choreography, spatial formations, costumes, and specific footwork are not described in the sources.

sections.origins_and_history: The Maypole Dance in Jamaica emerged during slavery and post-emancipation as one of the island's cultural traditions and dance forms that feature mento music.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Not described in sources, though elements of mento dance may be seen in Maypole performances.
sections.music_and_instruments: Maypole performances feature mento music, which typically includes acoustic instruments such as the acoustic guitar, banjo, hand drums, and the rhumba box.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance emerged during slavery and post-emancipation as part of Jamaica's cultural traditions.
sections.lineage: Linked to mento music and traditional Jamaican performance genres like quadrille and jonkunnu.
